what: An upload no longer re-does the whole corpus's index work. On 1,200 documents the index build went from 2.30s to 0.13s, and the index that comes out is asserted identical - field for field - to the one the previous implementation produced.

why_this_and_why_now.what_was_left: With parses cached and PDFs batched, re-indexing was the cost still paid on every upload and every delete, synchronously, inside the request the operator is waiting on.
why_this_and_why_now.measured_first: 400 documents (4,812 chunks) 1.04s; 1,200 (14,412) 3.42s; 2,400 (28,812) 7.23s. Linear, about 3ms a document - so five thousand policies is fifteen seconds of waiting after dragging in one file, and the file that changed is one of them.
why_this_and_why_now.where_it_went: Profiling put 79% of a warm re-index in the BM25 index build, and 35% of that in deriving tags - almost all of it tokenising the same unchanged documents again.

the_split.cached: Chunking a document, tokenising its passages, counting its words, its folded vocabulary and its tag sources depend on THAT DOCUMENT ALONE.
the_split.not_cached: The tf-idf ranking behind every document's tags, the corpus document frequencies, the average length and corpus_version are recomputed on every build. Adding one document changes what every other document's words are distinctive against; a cached tag set would be right on the day it was computed and quietly drift from then on. It is also the cheap half - the tokenising is what costs.
the_split.still_a_rebuild: What is reused is the work, not the result. A deleted document really does disappear: corpus_version, chunks and tags are all rebuilt from the current corpus, and a test asserts a removed document leaves no trace anywhere.

the_key.not_the_content_hash: content_hash covers document.text and was the obvious key. It is wrong twice. A Chunk carries allowed_principals, so an entry keyed on text alone could hand back a passage stamped with a folder's PREVIOUS audience - the worst mistake this product can make. And chunking reads blocks, not text: a heading rewritten as a paragraph with the same words leaves the text byte-identical and the passages different, because a heading starts a chunk and a paragraph does not.
the_key.what_it_costs: Hashing everything a chunk is made of - id, title, url, superseded, principals, text, and every block's kind, text, locator, level and heading trail - measured 22ms per 1,200 documents against the 2.3s it saves. There was nothing to trade off, so nothing was traded off.
the_key.the_chunk_window_too: target_words and overlap_words are in the key: the same document cut at a different width is a different set of passages, and an entry that ignored that would survive a settings change it should not have.

measured.one_upload_end_to_end: 400 documents 1.04s to 0.43s; 1,200 3.42s to 1.22s; 2,400 7.23s to 3.36s. About 2.2x, because the index build is no longer what dominates.
measured.memory: Measured twice and agreeing: the whole retriever went from 68.0 MB to 77.8 MB on 1,200 documents (21.9 MB of text), and the cache alone accounts for 9.8 MB of that - 14%. The chunks and counters are handed out by reference rather than copied, so the cache mostly holds what the index already holds.
measured.correctness: On a 150-document corpus of mixed formats in nested folders: the corpus document frequency is identical to the previous implementation's, every document's tags are identical to what the ORIGINAL derive_tags produced, and the whole index - chunks, term_freqs, lengths, doc_freq, avg_length, corpus_version, doc_principals, doc_tags, doc_tags_folded - is identical to the previous implementation's.

in_memory_on_purpose: Not written to disk, unlike the parse cache. This holds the index's own contents, so persisting it would roughly double the stored state to save a rebuild that now takes a fraction of a second. A restart pays one full derivation, from parses that are themselves cached.
three_tests_that_proved_nothing: Fourteen sabotages were applied to main and run. Three passed, and all three were the same mistake: the test compared the system against ITSELF. 'Warm cache equals cold cache' and 'the tags equal derive_tags' both move together when the derivation counts the wrong thing, so a chunk length that counted distinct terms instead of tokens, a document frequency built from only the last document, and a corpus vocabulary narrowed to taggable words all sailed through. They are now pinned against oracles computed by hand from the chunks - lengths against len(tokenize(chunk.text)), doc_freq against a Counter built from each chunk's distinct terms, and the corpus vocabulary against a two-document corpus with the short words spelled out. All fourteen fail against their bug now.
gate: No retrieval, prompt, chunking or grounding change: the same index, built from reused work. The index is asserted identical to the previous implementation's, field for field, on a real corpus. The golden sets gate answers, and no answer moved.
pinned_by: tests/test_derived_cache.py, 13 tests, plus one in tests/test_access_restamp.py for the sequence nothing covered: an admin walls off a folder, then somebody uploads and the corpus re-indexes. That rebuild reuses per-document work, and the one thing it must never reuse is who a passage belongs to. Confirmed to fail when principals are dropped from the key. 1,155 tests pass.
still_open: The bottleneck has moved to connector.fetch(), which is now most of an upload - 1.61s of the 3.36s at 2,400 documents. 64% of that is ParsedDocument.text normalising 22 MB through two regex passes at about 26 MB/s. Storing the normalised text in the parse cache would fix it and would grow that database by roughly the size of the corpus; not attempted, and worth deciding deliberately rather than by reflex.
a_check_of_mine_that_ran_nothing: The first run of that sabotage reported CAUGHT, from a subprocess whose sys.executable was the system python - no pytest installed, returncode 1, nothing executed. It showed as caught because a non-zero exit was being read as a failing test. Noticed from the shape of the output rather than the verdict: no test names, no summary line. Every sabotage runner now asserts that a summary line came back at all before believing the result.
a_caveat_added_later: The absolute seconds here are not reproducible between sessions. Measured again hours later on the same container and the same unchanged code, 'one upload' at 1,200 documents took 3.15s rather than the 1.22s recorded here - the box had since downloaded 2.6 GB of models and run two eval suites, and page cache and host contention are not controlled. The RATIOS in this record stand; treat the absolutes as one session's reading. Later records take every figure as a same-session A/B, restoring the shipped code from HEAD between runs.
